newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Zinc hits fresh highs, grain prices tumble.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Zinc hits fresh highs, grain prices tumble.

text.p: Industrial base metals notched up a volatile day on Monday with zinc hitting fresh, near seven-year highs while copper dipped sharply before staging a partial recovery.

Elsewhere in the commodity markets, U.S. grain prices came under strong pressure from favourable weather conditions in the Midwest and signs of a bumper summer harvest. Benchmark July wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Exchange were trading down five cents at $3.30.

Copper prices tumbled in London after breaking through a succession of technical support levels on follow-through selling from the metal's late slide on Friday which then set off a wave of stop-loss selling.
At its nadir, copper slid to $2,486 per tonne in the first ring of morning trading on the London Metal Exchange (LME) before managing to regain a firm grip above the $2,500 a tonne level.
Zinc continued a recent run-up fuelled by speculators seeking to capitalise on a healthy global economy by betting on a base metal with low producer and consumer stocks.
Inventory levels of zinc, which is used to galvanise steel and alloyed with copper to make brass, have consistently fallen at the LME, where they are down 15 percent since the start of the year.

But analysts have cautioned against the pace and extent of the price rise, warning that the market may have outpaced fundamentals. Zinc peaked at $1,415 a tonne before settling back in late LME trade to close at $1,411.

Cocoa prices received a strong boost as the market digested a report from the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission released after New York's close on Friday which showed a net gain in speculative long positions that was smaller than some had feared.
Worries about a possible strong jump in the reported figures had sent cocoa spinning on Friday, but benchmark September futures in London were up $20 to close Monday trading at $1,131.
Coffee suffered the reverse fate when it came under pressure after a private forecaster predicted Brazil's 1997/98 harvest to be well above the country's estimate.
Continuing mild weather in Brazil's coffee belt also discouraged potential buyers. London robusta coffee futures ended the day down $15 on the September at $1,845 per tonne.

On the precious metal front, gold suffered an early bout of weakness in London, threatening to sweep towards four-year lows before staging a rebound back near its opening levels. The Group of Seven conference over the weekend was seen bolstering the dollar, which helped explain gold's early weak performance.

Despite the day's mild recovery traders said the fundamental outlook remained negative for bullion. What flimsy support gold had was weakened late last week by news that the Belgian government proposed selling up to 133 tonnes of gold over five years in the form of commemorative coins beginning in 1999.
Gold ended the session lower in London at $338.45. per ounce versus $338.55 on Friday.
Platinum and palladium put in mixed and volatile performances with both moving in relatively wide ranges. The market remained preoccupied with confirmation of resumption of deliveries from Russia.

The country supplies 60 percent of world palladium needs and about 25 percent of platinum, but has been out the market since December because of internal wrangling over control of its metals industry.

In crude oil, mounting tension between the United Nations and Iraq sent prices higher after the U.N. adopted a resolution over the weekend threatening Iraq with further sanctions if it did not allow U.N. arms inspectors to search sensitive sites. Iraq has yet to begin the second part of a U.N. oil-for-food deal.
Bellwether London Brent for August delivery was up 13 cents at $17.80.
